facts.statement: The article title is "Oliver Mtukudzi: The Art of Protest".
The article URL is https://www.theelephant.info/analysis/2019/02/07/oliver-mtukudzi-the-art-of-protest/.
Mtukudzi made a conscious decision to push back against a musical invasion, seeking to preserve the Shona and Ndebele traditional sounds, leading to the birth of Tuku.
There are proponents who hold that, much as Mtukudzi worked overtime to become a Zimbabwean purist, he borrowed elements of his music from Benga.
The article states that the pushback illustrates Tuku's sense of eternal cultural patriotism.
Oliver Mtukudzi was born in September 1952 in Highfield, a Harare township.
Highfield is a Harare township with historic significance as one of the founding hotspots of Zimbabwe's independence movement.
Mtukudzi's parents met during a choir competition and passed down the music bug to their eldest son, Oliver, and his younger brother Robert.
Robert became a bandmate in Mtukudzi's Black Spirits.
In the early 1970s, the two brothers started experimenting with music and landed in trouble for sneaking out of the house to play at a local beer parlor.
At the beer parlor, Mtukudzi got a rare opportunity to have his first encounter with an electric guitar.
Mtukudzi's parents were against their two sons' pursuit of a career in music.
Mtukudzi recalled that he played the guitar so well that the following day those at the beer parlor reported to his father how talented he was.
Mtukudzi recalled that it was the one time his father hit him, for sneaking out of the house and spending time at the beer parlor in pursuit of music.
Mtukudzi was a self-taught guitarist who began experimenting, looking for his own unique sound that had observers saying he didn't play the guitar right.
Brighton Matebere was at the time a leading journalist with the Zimbabwe Broadcasting Corporation.
Brighton Matebere had a love interest on Mtukudzi's street and regularly ran into young Mtukudzi practicing with his guitar outside his family house whenever he came around to visit his girlfriend.
Matebere was impressed by Mtukudzi's skills and invited him to perform during his radio show.
Mtukudzi's impressive performance during the radio interview resulted in his first recording deal in 1975.
In 1977, Mtukudzi joined Wagon Wheel band, alongside Thomas Mapfumo.
Mtukudzi said, "When I left school I did not get a job for at least three years."

Mtukudzi said, "Blacks were not allowed to apply for jobs, but the colonialists didn't think of art as a weapon that could be used against them. So they allowed us to sing. It was therefore up to the artist to help the nation heal and grow. We used idioms and proverbs, knowing that Shona speakers would decipher the coded messages we were passing across without being explicitly political."
In 2016, Mtukudzi told Forbes Africa, "I am yet to decide on a career to take on, because this is not a career for me. I am just doing me."

In 2015, Mtukudzi said that Pakare Paye was his legacy, the legacy he was leaving behind for youngsters to get somewhere where they can showcase what they do best, and that his generation and he didn't have similar opportunities.
The Pakare Paye Arts Center means "that place".
The Pakare Paye Arts Center is an expansive piece of real estate which Mtukudzi transformed from a rundown junkyard into a state of the art facility with recording studios and performance spaces.
The Pakare Paye Arts Center is located in Norton, about 45 kms from Harare.
Pakare Paye has become a space for artistic apprentices seeking a soft landing in a country where the government gives little regard to the arts.
Pakare Paye remains a reminder of one of Mtukudzi's saddest memories, since he originally built it intending for his only son and bandmate, Sam, to run it.
Sam died from a 2010 road accident on his way from the airport.
Following his son's passing, Mtukudzi took a two year hiatus from recording music, returning with Sarawoga, meaning "left alone".
For now, the family musical baton rests with Selmour, Mtukudzi's daughter.
